name: TLV7163318PDPQR
title: TLV716, TLV716P: dual 150 mA capacitor-free LDO regulators in 1.2 mm × 1.2 mm X2SON-6
summary: Two independent fixed-voltage linear regulators sharing one input pin, each able to supply 150 mA, with output voltages offered from 1 V to 3.3 V. They run from 1.4 V to 5.5 V and are stable with no capacitor at the input or at either output; up to 100 µF may be added on each output. Each channel has its own enable pin, foldback current limit, inrush control, thermal shutdown and undervoltage lockout. The TLV716P versions add a 120 Ω pulldown that empties an output when its channel is disabled.
key_figures: 0.21 V typ, 0.42 V max at 150 mA, 3 V ≤ VOUT < 3.3 V
50 µA typ per channel at no load
80 dB at 100 Hz, 46 dB at 10 kHz

notes: The family names are TLV716 and TLV716P; both come only in the 6-pin X2SON (DPQ) package, body 1.20 mm × 1.20 mm nominal.
The TLV716P differs from the TLV716 only by the 120 Ω output pulldown switched in when a channel is disabled.

operation.text: Each channel has its own 0.8 V bandgap reference, undervoltage lockout, current limit and thermal shutdown, and a PMOS pass transistor from IN to its output; one enable and power-control logic block serves both channels from EN1 and EN2. On the TLV716P a 120 Ω resistor from each output to ground is switched in when that channel is off. The junction may run from -40 °C to 125 °C.

The control loop keeps both channels stable with no input or output capacitor, which saves parts and board area. Capacitors still improve AC behaviour: 0.1 µF or more on an output gives good dynamic response, and outputs may carry up to 100 µF. X5R and X7R ceramics are named for their small change of capacitance and ESR with temperature.

Not needed for stability. Fitting 0.1 µF to 1 µF between IN and ground offsets the impedance of the source and improves PSRR, ripple at the input and the response to supply steps. A larger value may be needed for big, fast load steps or when the supply is several inches away. A noisy supply benefits from extra low-ESR input capacitance for lower output noise; the supply should be well regulated with headroom above VOUT.

At power-up and on enable the output is charged with a constant current, so the load capacitance does not draw a surge that could trip the supply's overcurrent protection. With no output capacitor the inrush is lowest: in the two-rail example this keeps the input current under a 180 mA limit. Start-up time from EN to 98% of VOUT is 170 µs typ at 1 V and 900 µs typ at 3.3 V, both at 150 mA.

EN1 and EN2 are active high. A channel turns on above 0.9 V and off below 0.4 V; the low 0.9 V threshold suits GPIO from low-voltage processors. Where shutdown is not needed EN can be tied to IN. In shutdown each channel draws 0.1 µA typ. On the TLV716P the output is pulled down through 120 Ω once EN falls below 0.4 V, so an output capacitor discharges quickly.
Both outputs stay off until the input reaches about 1.3 V (typ), the point at which the internal circuits work properly.

The limit is 160 mA to 500 mA and folds back as the output falls; into a short the output current is 40 mA typ. While limiting, the output is not regulated and follows the load resistance. A sustained fault heats the die until thermal shutdown turns the channel off; it restarts on cooling, so a lasting fault makes the channel alternate between limiting and thermal turn-off.

The PMOS body diode conducts from OUT to IN whenever OUT is above IN, and that current is not limited. For extended reverse bias, limit it externally to 5% of rated output current; a Schottky diode with its anode on OUT and cathode on IN does this.

Below the dropout voltage the PMOS pass device runs in its linear region and looks like its RDS(ON) between IN and OUT, so dropout rises roughly in proportion to load current. PSRR and transient response worsen as VIN - VOUT nears dropout.

The output turns off at about 158 °C junction temperature and back on at about 140 °C, so under heavy dissipation it can cycle. Junction temperature is to be held at 125 °C or less; thermal shutdown sits 33 °C above that. To check margin, raise the ambient with worst-case load until shutdown trips. Running into thermal shutdown repeatedly reduces reliability.

Heat leaves through the board copper round the part; copper area free of other components, and heavier copper, carry more heat away. The thermal figures are for a JEDEC high-K board. Holding TJ at 125 °C with VIN = 5 V, VOUT1 = 3.3 V, VOUT2 = 1.8 V and IOUT2 = 0, the maximum ambient falls from 125 °C with no load to about 87 °C at IOUT1 = 150 mA, and with IOUT2 = 75 mA from about 89 °C to about 51 °C.

Any input and output capacitors go as close to the pins as possible. The recommended layout places COUT1 at OUT1 (pin 1) and COUT2 at OUT2 (pin 2) on the left side, CIN at IN (pin 5) on the right, with ground plane copper above and below the package.
The exposed pad on the underside is soldered to the board for thermal and mechanical performance; thermal vias can tie it to a copper plane that acts as the heatsink.
